Liver transplantation

Factors that have led to widening indications for transplantation are

transplantation
b) Living donor transplantation
c) Split-liver transplantation - liver is divided, usually into two unequal
parts, of which the highest returns to adult and lowest to a child
d) "domino" transplantation
e) Xenotransplantation - using as donor an animal, especially primates
2. Advances in immunology- Should be followed ABO system compatibility rule
- Preferable that donor and recipient have same blood type
- HLA compatibility in renal transplantation is very important, it plays no
role in liver transplants
3. Improvement in surgical
techniques		a) Extend of "piggyback" techniques without use of extracorporeal
circulation
- Used for whole liver transplantation in which implantation of IVC of
donors is made termino-lateral to IVC of receiver
b) Techniques with reduced liver transplant ("reduced size") used if
pediatric donors (by Bismuth)

transplantation
4. Deep studying of immune
tolerance

arteriography for the four main vessels)

book.html:
Organ transplantology – general aspects

Florin Graur, Emil Mois

Over the course of the last century, organ transplantation has overcome major technical limitations to become the success that is today and the results of organ transplantation continue to improve. In 1954 Dr. Joseph E. Murray from Boston made the first successful kidney transplant, while in 1966 Drs. Richard Lillehei from University of Minnesota made the first successful pancreas/kidney transplant. In 1968 Dr. Norman Shumway, Stanford University Hospital made the first successful heart transplant. Until the early 1980s, the potential of organ rejection limited the number of transplants performed. Medical advances in the prevention and treatment of rejection led to more successful transplants and an increase in demand. Transplantation medicine is one of the most challenging and complex areas of modern medicine.

Liver Transplantation

The first human liver transplant was performed by Starzl in 1963 in Denver (Colorado), but was no successful. Next patients with liver transplant done by him in the US and in England by Roy Calne, had the same fate, patients passing away. Only in 1967, Starzl managed the first liver transplant with patient survival. Introducing cyclosporin as immunosuppressant drug was an important moment in the history of liver transplantation.

Another important moment in the development of liver transplantation was the definition of brain death criteria in the late 60s, resulting in an expansion of indications and a remarkable increase in the number of operations carried out.

In Romania, liver transplant surgery began with experimental studies of S. V. Duca and V. Fluture. The first liver transplant was performed in Romania on June 21, 1997that was not followed by success and on April 15, 2000 the team headed by Prof. I. Popescu made the first liver transplant with patient survival.

Factors that have led to widening indications for transplantation are:

1. Increasing the number of donors:

a) use of expanded donors - has shown that age is not a factor in liver

transplantation

b) living donor transplantation

c) split-liver transplantation - liver is divided, usually into two unequal

parts, of which the highest returns to adult and lowest to a child

d) "domino" transplantation

e) xenotransplantation - using as donor an animal, especially primates.

2. Advances in immunology - should be followed the ABO system compatibility rule. It is even preferable that the donor and the recipient have the same blood type. The positive cross-match was not and is not presently a contraindication for liver transplantation. Although HLA compatibility in renal transplantation is very important, it plays no role in liver transplants.

3. Improvements in surgical techniques

a) extend of the"piggyback" techniques without the use of

extracorporeal circulation. This term is used for the whole liver

transplantation in which the implantation of inferior vena cava(IVC)

of the donors is made termino-lateral to the IVC of the receiver. Later

the term was extended to all liver transplant where the IVC of

receiver is preserved and full or partial liver is implanted termino-

lateral or latero-lateral.

b) techniques with reduced liver transplant ("reduced size") used if

pediatric donors. This technique introduced by Bismuth, has the

advantage to resolve pediatric cases that need urgent liver

transplantation, for which no suitable donor has been found. Since is

using a cadaver liver to a single recipient, this technique does not

contribute to increasing the number of donors. Yet is rarely practiced,

compared with split liver technique, which allows the use of both

liver segments.

4. In deep studying of the phenomenon of immune tolerance and improve it at the clinical level - it seems that after research led by T. Starzl, we might give up immunosuppression (adverse effects and the costs would be canceled).

In order to perform liver transplantation, it requires a comprehensive program which will include surgeons, anesthesiologists, therapists, gastroenterologists, radiologists, laboratory physicians, etc.

There are two major impediments in the development of a liver transplant program:

  • The number of donors, which is insufficient in most countries
  • The high cost of operation. Although at first glance, there are high costs of transplantation, with amounts ranging from 80,000 to 300,000 dollars, these amounts seem inferior to the costs of repeated hospitalizations in cirrhotic patients due to complications such as hepatic encephalopathy, gastrointestinal bleeding, primary peritonitis, ascites etc.

Brain death diagnosis

This concept is a delicate problem, being much debated lately. Perhaps the most important thing to understand is that brain death is equivalent to death of the patient, and this is what everyone should understand. The diagnosis of brain death involves three steps:

1. Determining the causes of the brain damage

2. Eliminating the causes that can simulate a brain death

(hypothermia, neuro-depressant drugs)

3. Clinical testing (includes 12 reflex absence) and paraclinical

(EEG, transcranialcerebral Doppler ultrasonography, cerebral

arteriography for the four main vessels).

Indications and contraindications for liver transplantation

They defined three major categories of indications:

  • Chronic liver disease in the terminal stage
  • Acute liver failure
  • Other metabolic liver diseases without therapeutic alternatives

Contraindications of liver transplantation are:

1. Absolute - HIV (some centers consider it as relative), uncontrolled sepsis, severe pulmonary hypertension, extrahepatic cancers, liver cancers, advanced active alcoholism or drug addiction, failure to comply with immunosuppressive therapy, irreversible brain damage (in failure liveracute).

2. Relative - portal vein thrombosis, hepatitis B antigen positive and HBe positive DNA, extreme ages, liver cancer, previous interventions o biliary tree.

Hepatic transplant involves:

1. Heterotopictransplant - with total liver;

  • with partial liver; 2. Orthotopic transplantation - with total liver;
  • liver part.

Orthotopic liver transplantation has become the only method of transplanting with long-term survival.

Technical liver transplantation with cadaver graft

The patient is placed supine on the table or both upper limbs in abduction to 90 ° or with only the left upper limb and right next to the body. The intervention is performed exclusively by abdominal access through bisubcostallaparotomy sometimes supplemented with a vertical midline incision ("Mercedes incision") or by a transverse (arcuate) abdominal incisionin children.

It starts with making the total hepatectomy of the receiver:

  • Hepatic pedicle dissection;
  • Liver mobilization by dissecting the round ligament, falciform ligament, coronary and triangular ligaments;
  • ICV isolation – suprahepatic and subhepaticsegments
  • Vascular exclusion of the liver
  • Ablation of liver;
  • Hemostasisafterhepatectomy.

If we are using a veno-venous "by-pass" a cannula is inserted in axillary vein, saphenous vein (usually the left) and portal vein.

Total orthotopic liver graft implantation involves two techniques:

1. The standard technique by

  • Suprahepatic ICV anastomosis performed by two running- sutures;
  • Subhepatic ICV anastomosis - anastomosis at this level is much easier. 2. Technical cavo-caval anastomosis with the cavalvein preservation involves:
  • Classic piggyback technique - In this case the orifice of the right hepatic vein can be tied or stapled off, and the common opening of the middle and left hepatic veins of the recipient are sewn to the donor’s suprahepatic IVC
  • Piggyback modifications - These were developed to allow preservation of caval flow, and to decrease venous outflow complications. Configurations include lateral side-to-side cavocavostomy and end-to-side cavocavostomy.
  • Triangulating cavocavostomy - It is similar to the variant of the piggyback technique described above but creates a much larger cavotomy. It combines the cavocavostomy incision with the orifice of the hepatic veins on both the donor and recipient. However, unlike the bicaval technique there is no need for retroperitoneal dissection of theIVC, nor is there a need for piggyback dissection

The next step involves making portal vein anastomosis and revascularization of the graft. The next are the arterial and biliary reconstruction.

On"reduced size" and “split-liver” transplant technique, the liver is divided into two parts that are used for two adult recipients.

Another alternative is living donation transplantation, in which part of the liver of a living donor is removed and transplanted. This technique is used mainly in children when segments II, and III are taken from a parent and transplanted.

Domino liver transplantation, wherein a patient who himself undergoes liver transplantation in turn donates his liver to another recipient.

Xenotransplantation involves the transplantation of a liver from an animal to human.

Specific complications of liver transplantation are:

1. Vascular complications: arterial thrombosis, vascular stenosis,

portal vein thrombosis, arterial aneurysms;

2. Biliary complications: biliary fistula, stenosis;

3. Postoperative: hemorrhage

General complications include: respiratory complications (pulmonary edema, ARDS, pleural effusion), hematologic (lymphoproliferative diseases in transplanted patients), Cushing syndrome, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, osteodystrophy.

Liver graft rejection are hyperacute, acute and chronic. Hyperacute rejection occurs rapidly – in minutes to hours - after transplantation being triggered by preformed antibodies. In acute rejection characteristic are the biliary epithelial lesions and intrahepatic biliary tract, manifested by inflammatory infiltrates. Among transplanted patients, 10-15% develops a chronic rejection with irreversible reaction of arterioles from portal space. To this is added vascular ischemia and hepatocellular necrosis. Vanishing bile duct syndrome although can be sometimes observed relatively quickly after transplant, is an important criteria for the diagnosis of chronic rejection.
